title: Standing firm
hook: those who say our Lord is Allah and then stand firm, the angels descend on them: don't fear (41:30)
tomorrow: Signs in the horizons and in themselves

segments.voice: Yesterday, repel with better, and your line was the same. Did someone hand you something sharp, and did you find something better to give back? Day five hundred sixty-five.

A companion named Sufyan ibn 'Abdullah comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with a request. Tell me something about Islam, he says, that I'll never need to ask anyone else about. One thing. Something to hold for the rest of my life. It's a big ask, and the answer, recorded in Sahih Muslim, is just two short sentences. The second one is a single word in Arabic, and it's the word Surah Fussilat puts at the center of today's verse.

Here's the answer. Say: I believe in Allah. Then be steadfast. Qul amantu billah, thumma staqim. Now hear Fussilat, verse thirty. Pickthall: "Lo! those who say: Our Lord is Allah, and afterward are upright, the angels descend upon them, saying: Fear not nor grieve, but hear good tidings of the paradise which ye are promised." The same two steps. Say it. Then stand firm. The word is istiqamah, from a root meaning to stand up straight, to be upright, like a pole that doesn't lean. Back on day four hundred thirty-three, we heard a report from Ibn 'Abbas that a command to stand firm, in Surah Hud, was harder on the Prophet than any other verse. Fussilat shows what's on the other side of it. Notice the order: the saying is quick, one sentence. The standing firm takes the rest of your life. Early Muslims explained it in their own ways. Abu Bakr is reported to have said it means not turning to anything besides Allah. 'Umar is reported to have said: stand straight on what you're commanded, and don't dodge around like a fox. And then the reward is not first a prize, but a presence. The angels descend, the verse says. Commentators say at death; some add the grave and the day of rising. And their first words are: don't be afraid, and don't grieve. In the verse, that's what follows steadiness: company in hard places, and two burdens lifted, the fear of what's coming and the grief for what's gone. A hadith in Bukhari adds the practical key: the deeds Allah loves most are the ones done constantly, even if they're small.

The practice: keep one practice steady. Sit up straight, spine upright, like a pole that doesn't lean. Breathe. Choose one small practice you already do, or this path itself, and decide to keep it going this week, every day, even on the days it feels like nothing. Make it small enough that you can't fail. Picture yourself doing it on your worst day. If you pray, ask for steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Istiqamah. Standing firm, upright, steadfast: what comes after saying our Lord is Allah, and what the angels meet with don't fear, don't grieve. Today's word.
Your line: say it, then stand firm. Today, do your one small practice even if you don't feel like it, and notice that doing it is the whole point. Day five hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims often quote the hadith 'say: I believe in Allah, then be steadfast' as a summary of the faith, and value small, regular acts of worship kept up over time.

myth: istiqamah means a single brave act
it means standing upright and staying that way, over time.
the angels' first words in 41:30 are don't fear and don't grieve
then good news of the garden that was promised.
a hadith says Allah loves the most constant deeds, even if small

fork.setup: you ask the Prophet: tell me one thing about Islam I'll never need to ask anyone else. what does he say?
options: say: I believe in Allah, then be steadfast.
fork.reveal: say: I believe in Allah, then be steadfast. two sentences, the same two steps as 41:30.

original.note: Arabic: standing firm, uprightness, from the root q-w-m, to stand.

trapdoor: what you thought: be strong when things get hard.
what it means: say your faith once, then stay upright in it for the rest of your life, and the angels meet you with don't fear.

what a scholar hears: 41:30 and Muslim 38 (Sufyan ibn 'Abdullah) share the pattern say, then istaqim; tafsir records Abu Bakr's and 'Umar's glosses; commentators place the angels' descent at death and, for some, in life.
